text: [Dyer v. Northbrook Property & Cas. Ins. Co. (1989) 210 CA3d 1540, 1547, 259 CR 298, 303] • [3:423] Nor does the employer's mistake or misunderstanding transfer a discharge into an “occurrence,” triggering the insurer's duty to defend: “The policy at issue defines ‘occurrence’ as accident; thus, any intentional conduct, i.e., termination, even if due to a misunderstanding, is not covered as an occurrence … An employment termination, even if due to mistake, cannot be unintentional.” [Lipson v. Jordache Enterprises, Inc. (1992) 9 CA4th 151, 159, 11 CR2d 271, 276 (emphasis added)] b. [3:424] Compare—post-termination torts: The result may be different where the tort claim is based on the insured employer's acts after the employee is discharged; e.g., defaming the ex-employee to a prospective new employer. However, an employment-related practices exclusion (see ¶ 3:318 ff.) may bar coverage even for post-termination tort claims. (See further discussion at ¶ 3:390 ff.) c.
